newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajikistan says guerrillas to free UN hostages.
newsitem.headline: Tajikistan says guerrillas to free UN hostages.

text.p: Tajikistan said on Saturday it had reached agreement with a rogue guerrilla group for the release of 23 hostages, including seven United Nations military observers held under threat of death.

In Moscow, meanwhile, separate talks aimed at ending Tajikistan's four-year civil war, between Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov and opposition delegation head Sayid Abdullo Nuri, continued without any apparent result.
Rakhmonov's press secretary, Zafar Saidov, told Itar-Tass news agency no peace accord would be signed on Saturday, as had been expected, and experts would try to prepare it by Monday.
"Both sides understand perfectly well that they should not be influenced by emotions," Saidov said.

"If the dialogue breaks down, the situation could become uncontrollable which would aggravate the military and political situation up to renewal of the war," he added. The negotiations are being mediated by Russia and the United Nations.

Amirkul Azimov, Secretary of Tajikistan's Security Council, told Reuters in the Tajik capital Dushanbe the guerrillas, who say they are loyal to field commander Rizvon Sadirov, had agreed to free all hostages after all-night talks.

He gave no details and did not say precisely where or when the hostages would be released. U.N. sources said its staff being held included two Bulgarians, a Dane, a Jordanian, a Ukrainian, a Uruguayan and an Austrian.

Sadirov had until recently been allied with the Islamic rebel opposition to Rakhmonov, but switched to back the government of the former Soviet republic, apparently without surrendering control of his forces.

A U.N. source in Dushanbe, capital of the former Soviet republic, told Reuters the guerrillas held up a column carrying U.N. personnel, Tajik officials and members of the armed Islamic opposition on Friday.

The hostage-takers demanded the rebels free Sadirov's brother, who is held by opposition fighters in the mountainous Tavildara region. Sadirov himself is believed to be in Afghanistan with groups of armed followers.
They also said Russian border guards, thousands of whom have a peacekeeping role in Tajikistan, must provide safe passage for Sadirov's fighters to join them from bases across the Afghan border.
They said they would shoot their hostages and detonate 30 bombs hidden around Dushanbe unless their demands were met by two p.m. (0900 GMT) on Sunday.
In New York, the U.N. Security Council members strongly condemned the seizure of hostages on Friday and appealed for their immediate release.
The U.N. mission has 96 foreign military observers in Tajikistan. Its mandate was renewed last week for four months.
U.N. observers have twice this month been subject to beatings or mock executions at the hands of Tajik government soldiers.
Tens of thousands of people have been killed in the civil war between Tajikistan's secular government and Islamist guerrillas.
Ceasefires agreed in the past have been routinely flouted, sometimes immediately after they were signed.
Russia, concerned about security on its volatile central Asian flank, has supported Rakhmonov's government but is also actively promoting peace talks with the opposition.
